sample/ask: A model answers a question by sampling. Asked seven times eight, it says fifty six half the time, fifty four three times in ten, and sixty four the rest: its probabilities, written with the Greek letter pi.
sample/reward: A checker scores each answer: a reward, R, of one when it is right and zero when it is wrong. It is just a number, with nothing to differentiate.
sample/goal: Training should raise the expected reward, J: the average R over the model's answers, here zero point five. Its gradient would say how to change the model's parameters, written theta.
sample/stuck: But theta reaches the reward only through which answer gets sampled, and a random draw has no slope.
trick/sum: Write the expected reward as a sum over every answer y: its probability, pi of y, times its reward, R of y. Only the probabilities depend on theta, so the gradient of J is each reward times the gradient of its probability.
trick/one: Take one answer and one parameter. Here theta is three scores, one per answer, through a softmax. theta zero is the first, the score of fifty six, whose probability is zero point five.
trick/nudge: Nudge theta zero up by zero point zero one, and pi of fifty six rises to zero point five oh two five: a slope of zero point two five, written partial pi, partial theta zero.
trick/chain: Now the slope of its log. ln pi is ln u, with pi as the inside, u. The slope of ln u is one over u, so by the chain rule, partial ln pi, partial theta zero is partial pi, partial theta zero divided by pi: zero point two five over zero point five, which is zero point five.
trick/back: Run it backwards: the slope of pi is pi times the slope of its log. zero point five times zero point five gives back zero point two five.
trick/trick: That holds for every answer and every parameter: the gradient of pi is pi times the gradient of ln pi. This is the log trick.
avg/avg: Put the trick into the gradient of J, and each answer brings R times the gradient of ln pi, weighted by its probability. For seven times eight: zero point five times one, times the gradient for fifty six, plus zero point three times zero, plus zero point two times zero.
avg/draws: A real model has far too many answers to list. But drawing answers weights them for free: fifty six turns up in half the draws. So R times the gradient of ln pi, averaged over answers drawn from the model, written y drawn from pi, is the gradient of J.
avg/est: Even one draw gives an estimate of it: the sampled answer's reward, times the gradient of its log-probability. That estimate is the policy gradient.
avg/eg: For fifty six, this model's gradient of ln pi is zero point five, minus zero point three, minus zero point two. Its first entry is the zero point five found for theta zero. With R equal to one, the estimate is that same vector.
push/up: Step theta a little along the estimate, and the log-probability of the sampled answer rises, in proportion to R. A rewarded fifty six becomes more likely.
push/zero: A wrong answer gets R of zero, so its estimate is zero, and nothing moves.
push/neg: A negative reward flips the step, and makes that answer less likely.
push/loss: As a loss to minimize, it is minus R times log pi of the sample: cross-entropy on the model's own answer, weighted by its reward.
push/p1: Try one. A checker gives minus one for a wrong answer, and the model samples fifty four. Its gradient of ln pi is minus zero point five, zero point seven, minus zero point two. What is the estimate?
push/a1: Multiply each entry by R. Minus one flips every sign: zero point five, minus zero point seven, zero point two. It points where fifty four gets less likely.
push/p2: Now average it with a second sample: fifty six, with R of one, whose estimate is zero point five, minus zero point three, minus zero point two.
push/a2: Add the two entry by entry: one, minus one, and zero. Then halve: zero point five, minus zero point five, and zero.
